claim: Female mosquitoes are attracted to human body heat during pursuit of a blood meal.
source: While most animals thermotax only to regulate their temperature, female mosquitoes are attracted to human body heat during pursuit of a blood meal.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about mosquito behavior.

claim: Host-seeking mosquitoes are maximally attracted to thermal stimuli approximating host body temperatures.
source: We show that host-seeking mosquitoes are maximally attracted to thermal stimuli approximating host body temperatures, seeking relative warmth while avoiding both relative cool and stimuli exceeding host body temperature.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Host-seeking mosquitoes seek relative warmth while avoiding both relative cool and stimuli exceeding host body temperature.
source: We show that host-seeking mosquitoes are maximally attracted to thermal stimuli approximating host body temperatures, seeking relative warmth while avoiding both relative cool and stimuli exceeding host body temperature.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: TRPA1 is required for specialized host-selective thermotaxis in mosquitoes.
source: We found that the cation channel TRPA1, in addition to playing a conserved role in thermoregulation and chemosensation, is required for this specialized host-selective thermotaxis in mosquitoes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mutant analysis data.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants failed to avoid stimuli exceeding host temperature during host-seeking.
source: During host-seeking, AaegTRPA1-/- mutants failed to avoid stimuli exceeding host temperature, and were unable to discriminate between host-temperature and high-temperature stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants were unable to discriminate between host-temperature and high-temperature stimuli.
source: During host-seeking, AaegTRPA1-/- mutants failed to avoid stimuli exceeding host temperature, and were unable to discriminate between host-temperature and high-temperature stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by choice assay data.

claim: TRPA1-dependent tuning of thermotaxis is likely critical for mosquitoes host-seeking in a complex thermal environment in which humans are warmer than ambient air, but cooler than surrounding sun-warmed surfaces.
source: TRPA1-dependent tuning of thermotaxis is likely critical for mosquitoes host-seeking in a complex thermal environment in which humans are warmer than ambient air, but cooler than surrounding sun-warmed surfaces.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the experimental data and ecological context.

claim: Adult Caenorhabditis elegans worms migrate preferentially toward a specific thermal environment determined by the temperature of their cultivation.
source: For instance, adult Caenorhabditis elegans worms migrate preferentially toward a specific thermal environment determined by the temperature of their cultivation (Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Adult Drosophila melanogaster flies prefer a narrow range of air temperatures around 24–25°C.
source: Adult Drosophila melanogaster flies prefer a narrow range of air temperatures around 24–25°C (Sayeed and Benzer, 1996; Hamada et al., 2008) and rapidly avoid air temperatures of ~31°C (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Adult Drosophila melanogaster flies rapidly avoid air temperatures of ~31°C.
source: Adult Drosophila melanogaster flies prefer a narrow range of air temperatures around 24–25°C (Sayeed and Benzer, 1996; Hamada et al., 2008) and rapidly avoid air temperatures of ~31°C (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some hematophagous arthropods have evolved a specialized mode of thermotaxis to locate endothermic hosts.
source: Interestingly, some hematophagous (blood-feeding) arthropods have evolved a specialized mode of thermotaxis to locate endothermic (warm-blooded) hosts.
evidence: This is supported by examples and citations provided in the following sentence.

claim: Thermophilic behavior is seen in kissing bugs Triatoma infestans and Rhodnius prolixus.
source: Such thermophilic behavior is seen in kissing bugs [Triatoma infestans (Flores and Lazzari, 1996) and Rhodnius prolixus (Schmitz et al., 2000)], the bedbug [Cimex lectularius (Rivnai, 1931)], the tick [Ixodes ricinus (Lees, 1948)], and many species of mosquito (Clements, 1999) including Ae. aegypti, a major tropical disease-vector (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilic behavior is seen in the bedbug Cimex lectularius.
source: Such thermophilic behavior is seen in kissing bugs [Triatoma infestans (Flores and Lazzari, 1996) and Rhodnius prolixus (Schmitz et al., 2000)], the bedbug [Cimex lectularius (Rivnai, 1931)], the tick [Ixodes ricinus (Lees, 1948)], and many species of mosquito (Clements, 1999) including Ae. aegypti, a major tropical disease-vector (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilic behavior is seen in the tick Ixodes ricinus.
source: Such thermophilic behavior is seen in kissing bugs [Triatoma infestans (Flores and Lazzari, 1996) and Rhodnius prolixus (Schmitz et al., 2000)], the bedbug [Cimex lectularius (Rivnai, 1931)], the tick [Ixodes ricinus (Lees, 1948)], and many species of mosquito (Clements, 1999) including Ae. aegypti, a major tropical disease-vector (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermophilic behavior is seen in many species of mosquito including Ae. aegypti.
source: Such thermophilic behavior is seen in kissing bugs [Triatoma infestans (Flores and Lazzari, 1996) and Rhodnius prolixus (Schmitz et al., 2000)], the bedbug [Cimex lectularius (Rivnai, 1931)], the tick [Ixodes ricinus (Lees, 1948)], and many species of mosquito (Clements, 1999) including Ae. aegypti, a major tropical disease-vector (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ae. aegypti is a major tropical disease-vector.
source: Such thermophilic behavior is seen in kissing bugs [Triatoma infestans (Flores and Lazzari, 1996) and Rhodnius prolixus (Schmitz et al., 2000)], the bedbug [Cimex lectularius (Rivnai, 1931)], the tick [Ixodes ricinus (Lees, 1948)], and many species of mosquito (Clements, 1999) including Ae. aegypti, a major tropical disease-vector (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Female Ae. aegypti require a vertebrate blood meal for the production of eggs.
source: Female Ae. aegypti require a vertebrate blood meal for the production of eggs, and finding a suitable warm-blooded host is therefore an essential component of reproduction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mosquito biology.

claim: Finding a suitable warm-blooded host is an essential component of reproduction for female Ae. aegypti.
source: Female Ae. aegypti require a vertebrate blood meal for the production of eggs, and finding a suitable warm-blooded host is therefore an essential component of reproduction.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the requirement for blood meals for egg production.

claim: Mosquitoes use a variety of physical and chemical senses to locate hosts in their environment.
source: Mosquitoes use a variety of physical and chemical senses to locate hosts in their environment (Cardé, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: When host-seeking, mosquitoes become strongly attracted to inanimate warm objects, eagerly probing at them as if they were hosts.
source: When host-seeking, these animals become strongly attracted to inanimate warm objects, eagerly probing at them as if they were hosts (Howlett, 1910).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Host-seeking behavior in Ae. aegypti can be activated by an increase in ambient carbon dioxide.
source: For mosquitoes such as Ae. aegypti, host-seeking behavior can be activated by an increase in ambient carbon dioxide (CO2) (Majeed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CO2 activation elicits flight activity in Ae. aegypti.
source: This activation elicits flight activity (Eiras and Jepson, 1991; McMeniman et al., 2014) and results in an array of behaviors including attraction to visual stimuli (van Breugel et al., 2015) and host olfactory cues (Dekker et al., 2005; McMeniman et al., 2014), and landing on warm objects (Burgess, 1959; Eiras and Jepson, 1994; Kröber et al., 2010; Maekawa et al., 2011; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CO2 activation results in attraction to visual stimuli in Ae. aegypti.
source: This activation elicits flight activity (Eiras and Jepson, 1991; McMeniman et al., 2014) and results in an array of behaviors including attraction to visual stimuli (van Breugel et al., 2015) and host olfactory cues (Dekker et al., 2005; McMeniman et al., 2014), and landing on warm objects (Burgess, 1959; Eiras and Jepson, 1994; Kröber et al., 2010; Maekawa et al., 2011; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CO2 activation results in attraction to host olfactory cues in Ae. aegypti.
source: This activation elicits flight activity (Eiras and Jepson, 1991; McMeniman et al., 2014) and results in an array of behaviors including attraction to visual stimuli (van Breugel et al., 2015) and host olfactory cues (Dekker et al., 2005; McMeniman et al., 2014), and landing on warm objects (Burgess, 1959; Eiras and Jepson, 1994; Kröber et al., 2010; Maekawa et al., 2011; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CO2 activation results in landing on warm objects in Ae. aegypti.
source: This activation elicits flight activity (Eiras and Jepson, 1991; McMeniman et al., 2014) and results in an array of behaviors including attraction to visual stimuli (van Breugel et al., 2015) and host olfactory cues (Dekker et al., 2005; McMeniman et al., 2014), and landing on warm objects (Burgess, 1959; Eiras and Jepson, 1994; Kröber et al., 2010; Maekawa et al., 2011; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ae. aegypti flying in a wind tunnel can detect a warmed stimulus from a distance, eliciting attraction and thermotaxis.
source: Ae. aegypti flying in a wind tunnel can detect a warmed stimulus from a distance, eliciting attraction and thermotaxis (van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Thermotaxis is typically initiated by thermosensitive neurons that sample environmental temperature to inform navigational decision-making.
source: Thermotaxis is typically initiated by thermosensitive neurons that sample environmental temperature to inform navigational decision-making.
evidence: This is established knowledge about thermotaxis mechanisms.

claim: Thermosensitive neurons must be equipped with molecular thermosensors capable of detecting and transducing thermal stimuli.
source: Such neurons must be equipped with molecular thermosensors capable of detecting and transducing thermal stimuli.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the function of thermosensitive neurons.

claim: Many molecular thermoreceptors are members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) superfamily of ion channels.
source: Diverse molecular thermoreceptors have been identified in the animal kingdom, many of which are members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) superfamily of ion channels (Barbagallo and Garrity, 2015; Palkar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different thermosensitive TRPs show distinct tuning spanning the thermal spectrum from noxious cold to noxious heat.
source: Different thermosensitive TRPs show distinct tuning spanning the thermal spectrum from noxious cold to noxious heat.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRP channel properties.

claim: TRPA1 is a heat sensor in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Among these is TRPA1, which is a heat sensor in multiple insects, including the vinegar fly D. melanogaster and the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae (Hamada et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TRPA1 is a heat sensor in Anopheles gambiae.
source: Among these is TRPA1, which is a heat sensor in multiple insects, including the vinegar fly D. melanogaster and the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae (Hamada et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons in thermosensitive sensilla of An. gambiae female antennae express TRPA1.
source: Neurons in thermosensitive sensilla (Gingl et al., 2005) of An. gambiae female antennae express TRPA1 (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In D. melanogaster, TRPA1 is expressed in internal thermosensors located in the brain.
source: In D. melanogaster, TRPA1 is expressed in internal thermosensors located in the brain, and DmelTRPA1-/- mutants fail to avoid high air temperature in a thermal gradient (Hamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: DmelTRPA1-/- mutants fail to avoid high air temperature in a thermal gradient.
source: In D. melanogaster, TRPA1 is expressed in internal thermosensors located in the brain, and DmelTRPA1-/- mutants fail to avoid high air temperature in a thermal gradient (Hamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some snakes and vampire bats express thermosensitive TRP channels in organs used to sense infrared radiation from warm-blooded prey.
source: Interestingly, some snakes and vampire bats express thermosensitive TRP channels in organs used to sense infrared radiation from warm-blooded prey (Gracheva et al., 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gr28b is a gustatory receptor paralog expressed in heat-sensitive neurons of D. melanogaster aristae.
source: Recently, a structurally distinct insect thermosensor, Gr28b, was identified in D. melanogaster (Ni et al., 2013). Gr28b, a gustatory receptor paralog, is expressed in heat-sensitive neurons of D. melanogaster aristae and is an important component of thermotaxis during rapid avoidance of heat (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gr28b is an important component of thermotaxis during rapid avoidance of heat in D. melanogaster.
source: Recently, a structurally distinct insect thermosensor, Gr28b, was identified in D. melanogaster (Ni et al., 2013). Gr28b, a gustatory receptor paralog, is expressed in heat-sensitive neurons of D. melanogaster aristae and is an important component of thermotaxis during rapid avoidance of heat (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gr28b is highly conserved among Drosophila species.
source: It is also highly conserved among Drosophila species (McBride et al., 2007), and has a clear ortholog in Ae. aegypti, AaegGr19 (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gr28b has a clear ortholog in Ae. aegypti, AaegGr19.
source: It is also highly conserved among Drosophila species (McBride et al., 2007), and has a clear ortholog in Ae. aegypti, AaegGr19 (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ae. aegypti mosquitoes reliably responded to 12 serial presentations of a 3-minute long 40°C stimulus over the course of more than 2.5 hr, with no evidence of habituation.
source: In our heat-seeking assay, Ae. aegypti mosquitoes reliably responded to 12 serial presentations of a 3-minute long 40°C stimulus over the course of more than 2.5 hr, with no evidence of habituation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ae. aegypti can feed on a variety of hosts with core body temperatures ranging from ~37°C (humans) to ~40–43°C (chickens).
source: Ae. aegypti can feed on a variety of hosts (Clements, 1999; Tandon and Ray, 2000) with core body temperatures ranging from ~37°C (humans) to ~40–43°C (chickens) (Richards, 1971) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Mosquitoes were highly sensitive to thermal contrast and were attracted to stimuli 2.5°C above ambient.
source: We found that mosquitoes were highly sensitive to thermal contrast and were attracted to stimuli 2.5°C above ambient (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: Mosquito occupancy on the Peltier increased monotonically with stimulus temperatures up to 40°C.
source: Furthermore, mosquito occupancy on the Peltier increased monotonically with stimulus temperatures up to 40°C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: For higher temperature stimuli above 40°C, there was a dramatic reduction in Peltier occupancy.
source: However, for higher temperature stimuli, we observed a dramatic reduction in Peltier occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: A 50°C stimulus resulted in approximately half as many animals on the Peltier compared to a 40°C stimulus.
source: A 50°C stimulus resulted in approximately half as many animals on the Peltier compared to a 40°C stimulus (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: Stimuli of 55°C or greater resulted in occupancy rates indistinguishable from an ambient thermal stimulus (26°C).
source: Stimuli of 55°C or greater resulted in occupancy rates indistinguishable from an ambient thermal stimulus (26°C) (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: While mosquitoes were still attracted to high-temperature stimuli, they populated the area peripheral to the Peltier, and strongly avoided the Peltier itself for stimuli ≥ 55°C.
source: Spatial analysis of mosquito occupancy on or near the Peltier revealed that while mosquitoes were still attracted to high-temperature stimuli, they populated the area peripheral to the Peltier, and strongly avoided the Peltier itself for stimuli ≥ 55°C (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Peltier occupancy for stimuli 21–40°C depended on the differential between the Peltier and ambient temperature, rather than the absolute temperature of the Peltier.
source: We found that Peltier occupancy for stimuli 21–40°C depended on the differential between the Peltier and ambient temperature (Figures 2B,C), rather than the absolute temperature of the Peltier (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A–C.

claim: At all ambient temperatures tested, a stimulus 5°C above ambient was sufficient to elicit significant heat-seeking.
source: For example, at all ambient temperatures tested, a stimulus 5°C above ambient was sufficient to elicit significant heat-seeking, and elicited approximately half as much Peltier occupancy as a stimulus 10°C above ambient.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A stimulus 5°C above ambient elicited approximately half as much Peltier occupancy as a stimulus 10°C above ambient.
source: For example, at all ambient temperatures tested, a stimulus 5°C above ambient was sufficient to elicit significant heat-seeking, and elicited approximately half as much Peltier occupancy as a stimulus 10°C above ambient.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Heat-seeking to targets 50–55°C was inhibited at all ambient temperatures tested.
source: On the other hand, heat-seeking to targets 50–55°C was inhibited at all ambient temperatures tested (Figures 2D,F), despite the fact that the temperature differential varied widely in these situations (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D–F.

claim: Ae. aegypti thermotaxis is driven by seeking relative warmth, but restricted by an absolute upper threshold of ~50–55°C.
source: These results show that Ae. aegypti thermotaxis is driven by seeking relative warmth, but restricted by an absolute upper threshold of ~50–55°C.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Mosquitoes left the Peltier at similar rates regardless of the absolute temperature of the stimulus.
source: We found that mosquitoes left the Peltier at similar rates regardless of the absolute temperature of the stimulus (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; based on analysis of data in Figure 1D,E), demonstrating that mosquitoes avoid relative cool during heat-seeking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mosquitoes avoid relative cool during heat-seeking.
source: We found that mosquitoes left the Peltier at similar rates regardless of the absolute temperature of the stimulus (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; based on analysis of data in Figure 1D,E), demonstrating that mosquitoes avoid relative cool during heat-seeking.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing similar rates of leaving the Peltier.

claim: Ae. aegypti heat-seeking involves seeking of relative warmth, avoidance of relative cool, and avoidance of thermal stimuli exceeding host temperature.
source: Our characterization of Ae. aegypti heat-seeking revealed multiple behavioral components contributing to selective thermotaxis during host-seeking: 1) the seeking of relative warmth; 2) the avoidance of relative cool; and 3) the avoidance of thermal stimuli exceeding host temperature.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the thermotaxis assays.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants rejected denatonium benzoate.
source: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants rejected denatonium benzoate (Figure 3D) but did not avoid consumption of N-methylmaleimide (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants did not avoid consumption of N-methylmaleimide.
source: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants rejected denatonium benzoate (Figure 3D) but did not avoid consumption of N-methylmaleimide (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild-type Ae. aegypti mosquitoes strongly avoided consumption of N-methylmaleimide.
source: Using a modified capillary feeding (CAFE) assay (Ja et al., 2007) (Figure 3B), we found that wild-type Ae. aegypti mosquitoes strongly avoided consumption of N-methylmaleimide (Figure 3C), as well as the bitter compound denatonium benzoate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild-type Ae. aegypti mosquitoes strongly avoided consumption of denatonium benzoate.
source: Using a modified capillary feeding (CAFE) assay (Ja et al., 2007) (Figure 3B), we found that wild-type Ae. aegypti mosquitoes strongly avoided consumption of N-methylmaleimide (Figure 3C), as well as the bitter compound denatonium benzoate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TRPA1 is a highly conserved chemosensor of electrophile irritants such as N-methylmaleimide.
source: In addition to its function as a thermoreceptor, TRPA1 is a highly conserved chemosensor of electrophile irritants such as N-methylmaleimide (Macpherson et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants were impaired in avoidance of high air temperature, leading to significant mortality.
source: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants were impaired in avoidance of high air temperature, leading to significant mortality (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: TRPA1 has a conserved chemosensory and thermosensory function in Ae. aegypti.
source: Together, these data indicate that TRPA1 has a conserved chemosensory and thermosensory function in Ae. aegypti.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the N-methylmaleimide avoidance and thermal gradient assay data.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants showed normal attraction to stimuli at or below 45°C.
source: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants showed normal attraction to stimuli at or below 45°C, but strikingly lacked normal avoidance of higher temperature stimuli (50°C and 55°C) (Figures 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E,F.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants lacked normal avoidance of higher temperature stimuli (50°C and 55°C).
source: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants showed normal attraction to stimuli at or below 45°C, but strikingly lacked normal avoidance of higher temperature stimuli (50°C and 55°C) (Figures 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E,F.

claim: AaegTRPA1-/- mutants persisted on the Peltier during 50, 55, and 60°C stimulus presentations, whereas control animals rapidly left these high-temperature stimuli.
source: A detailed analysis of Peltier occupancy over time revealed that AaegTRPA1-/- mutants persisted on the Peltier during 50, 55, and 60°C stimulus presentations, whereas control animals rapidly left these high-temperature stimuli (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: AaegTRPA1 is not required for initial attraction to warmth but is required for normal avoidance of high-temperature stimuli that exceed host body temperature.
source: Therefore, AaegTRPA1 is not required for initial attraction to warmth but is required for normal avoidance of high-temperature stimuli that exceed host body temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 3E–G.

claim: AaegGr19-/- mutant mosquitoes showed no thermotaxis defects.
source: Although this thermosensor is required for mediating rapid avoidance of warmth in D. melanogaster (Ni et al., 2013), AaegGr19-/- mutant mosquitoes showed no thermotaxis defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Gr28b is required for mediating rapid avoidance of warmth in D. melanogaster.
source: Although this thermosensor is required for mediating rapid avoidance of warmth in D. melanogaster (Ni et al., 2013), AaegGr19-/- mutant mosquitoes showed no thermotaxis defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: DmelTRPA1 is expressed in internal thermosensors of the brain.
source: DmelTRPA1 is expressed in internal thermosensors of the brain (Hamada et al., 2008), while thermosensitive isoforms of DmelGr28b are expressed in peripheral heat-sensors (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Thermosensitive isoforms of DmelGr28b are expressed in peripheral heat-sensors.
source: DmelTRPA1 is expressed in internal thermosensors of the brain (Hamada et al., 2008), while thermosensitive isoforms of DmelGr28b are expressed in peripheral heat-sensors (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: TRPA1 RNA is expressed in numerous tissues including the antennae in Ae. aegypti.
source: In Ae. aegypti, TRPA1 RNA is expressed in numerous tissues including the antennae (Matthews et al., 2015), where it may be associated with peripheral thermosensitive sensilla responding to rapid thermal fluctuations (Gingl et al., 2005), as it is in An. gambiae (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: TRPA1 may be associated with peripheral thermosensitive sensilla responding to rapid thermal fluctuations in Ae. aegypti.
source: In Ae. aegypti, TRPA1 RNA is expressed in numerous tissues including the antennae (Matthews et al., 2015), where it may be associated with peripheral thermosensitive sensilla responding to rapid thermal fluctuations (Gingl et al., 2005), as it is in An. gambiae (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation based on expression data and comparison to An. gambiae.

claim: Gr19 transcript is broadly expressed in Ae. aegypti.
source: The cellular expression pattern of Gr19 in Ae. aegypti is not known, but its transcript is broadly expressed (Matthews et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: When presented with two 40°C stimuli, both wild-type and mutant mosquitoes distributed equally between the Peltiers.
source: When presented with two 40°C stimuli, both wild-type and mutant mosquitoes distributed equally between the Peltiers (Figure 4B), but in a choice between a 40°C and 50°C stimulus, wild-type mosquitoes strongly preferred the 40°C Peltier (Figure 4C) and avoided the 50°C Peltier (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In a choice between a 40°C and 50°C stimulus, wild-type mosquitoes strongly preferred the 40°C Peltier.
source: When presented with two 40°C stimuli, both wild-type and mutant mosquitoes distributed equally between the Peltiers (Figure 4B), but in a choice between a 40°C and 50°C stimulus, wild-type mosquitoes strongly preferred the 40°C Peltier (Figure 4C) and avoided the 50°C Peltier (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In a choice between a 40°C and 50°C stimulus, wild-type mosquitoes avoided the 50°C Peltier.
source: When presented with two 40°C stimuli, both wild-type and mutant mosquitoes distributed equally between the Peltiers (Figure 4B), but in a choice between a 40°C and 50°C stimulus, wild-type mosquitoes strongly preferred the 40°C Peltier (Figure 4C) and avoided the 50°C Peltier (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In a choice between a 40°C and 50°C stimulus, AaegTRPA1-/- mutants failed to avoid the 50°C Peltier, resulting in no preference for the 40°C stimulus.
source: Remarkably, in this choice scenario, AaegTRPA1-/- mutants failed to avoid the 50°C Peltier, resulting in no preference for the 40°C stimulus (Figure 4 C, D, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C,D and Video 1.

claim: In an outdoor environment, hosts are often warmer than the surrounding air but cooler than sun-warmed soil, rocks, trees, and human-made objects.
source: In an outdoor environment, however, hosts are often warmer than the surrounding air but cooler than sun-warmed soil, rocks, trees, and human-made objects (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is illustrated by the thermal image in Figure 4F.

claim: Diurnal mosquitoes such as Ae. aegypti are poorly served by merely thermotaxing to the hottest object available.
source: For this reason, diurnal mosquitoes such as Ae. aegypti are poorly served by merely thermotaxing to the hottest object available.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the thermal landscape described.

claim: A more optimal strategy for mosquitoes is to search specifically for biologically relevant stimuli, and to avoid thermal stimuli exceeding host temperature.
source: A more optimal strategy is to search specifically for biologically relevant stimuli, and to avoid thermal stimuli exceeding host temperature, as we have observed in our laboratory models of heat-seeking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and ecological context.

claim: Acquiring a blood meal is an essential component of reproduction for a female Ae. aegypti mosquito.
source: Acquiring a blood meal is an essential component of reproduction for a female Ae. aegypti mosquito.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mosquito biology.

claim: Both AaegTRPA1-/- and AaegGr19-/- mutants retain normal attraction to warmth.
source: Our work identifies TRPA1 as a gene regulating mosquito avoidance of high-temperature stimuli, which we have shown to be a major behavioral component of heat-seeking. However, because both AaegTRPA1-/- and AaegGr19-/- mutants retain normal attraction to warmth, this aspect of heat-seeking must rely on other thermoreceptors, still to be identified.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing normal attraction to warmth in both mutants.
